```{r}
notes_theme = theme_minimal(base_size = 14, base_family = "Source Sans 3")
theme_set(notes_theme)

regression_panel <- function(formula, scat.formula = NULL, data, xlab, ylab) {
  mod <- lm(formula, data = data)
  
  aug <- augment(mod)
  
  plot_fit <- makeFun(mod)
  
  if(is.null(scat.formula)) {
    orig_data <- gf_point(formula, data = data, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, color = "#003300")
  } else {
    orig_data <- gf_point(scat.formula, data = data, xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, color = "#003300") 
  }
  
  orig_data <- orig_data %>% gf_fun(plot_fit(x) ~ x, color = "#f15a31")
  
  resid_plot <- gf_point(.std.resid ~ .fitted, data = aug, xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Standardized residuals") %>%
    gf_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "#f15a31")
  
  qq_plot <- gf_qq(~.std.resid, data = aug, xlab = "N(0,1) quantiles", ylab = "Standardized residuals", color = "#003300") %>%
    gf_qqline(color = "#f15a31")
  
  (orig_data | resid_plot | qq_plot)
}


bikes_mlr <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual*weekend, data = bikes)
```

## Running Example

This dataset has information on 150 news articles, some that are real and some that are fake. Our goal is to build a statistical model to explain `type` based on features of the article

- `type`: "real" or "fake" / `type_num`: 0 (real) or 1 (fake)
- `title` and `url` of article
- `title_words`: how many words in the title
- `title_has_excl`: whether title has exclamation
- `title_caps_percent`: percent of title in capital letters
- `negative`: Percent of words that have negative sentiment
- `positive`: Percent of words that have positive sentiment

## 

::: small

```{r}
news <- bayesrules::fake_news |>
  select(title, url, type, title_words, title_has_excl, title_caps_percent, negative, positive) |>
  mutate(type_num = as.numeric(type == "fake"))

write_csv(news, here("data/fake_news_bayesrules.csv"))

knitr::kable(head(news))
```

:::

## Fake news model (from activity)


```{r}
news_mod <- glm(type_num ~ title_words + title_has_excl + title_caps_percent, 
                data = news, family = "binomial")
```


## Fitted regression model: 3 scales


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%" .small}
$\log(\frac{\widehat p}{1-\widehat p}) = \widehat\beta_0 + \widehat\beta_1 x$
:::

::: {.column width="33%" .small}
$\text{odds}(x) = e^{\widehat\beta_0 + \widehat\beta_1 x}$
:::

::: {.column width="33%" .small}
$P(Y = 1 | x) = \frac{e^{\widehat\beta_0 + \widehat\beta_1 x}}{1 + e^{\widehat\beta_0 + \widehat\beta_1 x}}$
:::
::::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4
tibble(
  x = seq(0, 60, by = .5),
  log_odds = -0.9318 + 0.09772 * x,
  odds = exp(log_odds),
  prob = exp(log_odds)/(1 + exp(log_odds))
) |>
  pivot_longer(-x) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = value)) + 
  geom_line(color = "#003300", linewidth = 1.5) + 
  facet_wrap(vars(name), scales = "free_y") + 
  labs(y = "")
```

## Logistic regression: linear predictor with a logit link function

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%" .small}
$\widehat \eta = \log(\frac{\widehat p}{1-\widehat p}) = \widehat\beta_0 + \widehat\beta_1 x$
:::

::: {.column width="33%" .small}
Link function: logit

$\widehat \eta \to P(Y=1)$
:::

::: {.column width="33%" .small}
$P(Y = 1 | x) = \frac{e^{\widehat\beta_0 + \widehat\beta_1 x}}{1 + e^{\widehat\beta_0 + \widehat\beta_1 x}}$
:::
::::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4
tibble(
  x = seq(0, 60, by = .5),
  log_odds = -0.9318 + 0.09772 * x,
  #odds = exp(log_odds),
  prob = exp(log_odds)/(1 + exp(log_odds))
) |>
  pivot_longer(-x) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = value)) + 
  geom_line(color = "#003300", linewidth = 1.5) + 
  facet_wrap(vars(name), scales = "free_y") + 
  labs(y = "")
```

## Linear regression: linear predictor with an identity link function

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%" .small}
$\widehat \eta = \widehat y = \widehat\beta_0 + \widehat\beta_1 x$
:::

::: {.column width="33%" .small}
Link function: identity

$f(\eta) = \eta$
:::

::: {.column width="33%" .small}
$\widehat y= \widehat \beta_0 + \widehat \beta_1 x$
:::
::::

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4
tibble(
  x = seq(0, 60, by = .5),
  eta = -0.9318 + 0.09772 * x,
  y_hat = eta,
  #odds = exp(log_odds),
  #prob = exp(log_odds)/(1 + exp(log_odds))
) |>
  pivot_longer(-x) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = value)) + 
  geom_line(color = "#003300", linewidth = 1.5) + 
  facet_wrap(vars(name), scales = "free_y") + 
  labs(y = "")

```


## Generalized linear model

<br>

**Linear Predictor**

$\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + ... + \beta_p x_p$

<br>

**Link Function**

$\theta = g(\eta)$

<br>

**Response distribution**

$Y$ is a random variable with mean $\theta$

## Binary logistic regression

If $Y$ follows a Bernoulli distribution

$${\rm E}(Y | X) = \pi(X)$$

We link this mean function to the explanatory variables using the logit link

\begin{align*}
\eta &= {\rm logit}(\pi(X))\\ 
&= \log \left( \dfrac{\pi(X)}{1 - \pi(X)} \right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p
\end{align*}



# Wald-based inference 

## Maximum likelihood (ML) estimation {.smaller}

The coefficients in logistic regression are estimated by finding the $\widehat{\beta}_0, \ldots, \widehat{\beta}_p$ that maximize the probability of the observed outcomes



$$L(\beta) = P(Y_1 = y_1, \ldots Y_n = y_n | \beta, X) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \pi(X)^{y_i} \Big[ 1 - \pi(X) \Big]^{1- y_i}$$


where

$$\pi(X) = \dfrac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \cdots + \beta_p X_p}}$$

::: footer
For more, consider taking Stat250! 
:::



## Properties of ML estimators 

If the sample is large and the model is correct, the ML estimator $\hat\beta_i$ is: 

1. Essentially unbiased

1. SEs can be computed and are about as small as any other unbiased estimator

1. The sampling distributions for the estimators are approximately **normal**

::: footer
For more, consider taking Stat250! 
:::

## Wald test for a coefficient 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}
**Hypotheses:**
:::

::: {.column width="75%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
$H_0: \beta_i = 0 \quad$ vs. $\quad H_a: \beta_i \ne 0$
:::
:::

::::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}
**Test statistic:**
:::

::: {.column width="75%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
$z = \dfrac{\widehat{\beta}_i}{SE(\widehat{\beta}_i)}$
:::
:::

::::

<br>


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}
**Reference distribution:**
:::

::: {.column width="75%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
$N(0, 1)$
:::
:::

::::




## CI for a coefficient 

A normal-based confidence interval for ${\beta}_i$

$$\widehat{\beta}_i \pm z^*_{1-\alpha/2} SE(\widehat{\beta}_i)$$

. . .

CI for the multiplicative effect on odds of success for a 1- unit change in $x$ (odds ratio of Success for $x+1$ vs. $x$):

$$e^{\widehat{\beta}_i - z^*_{1-\alpha/2} SE(\widehat{\beta}_i)} \quad \text{to} \quad e^{\widehat{\beta}_i + z^*_{1-\alpha/2} SE(\widehat{\beta}_i)}$$

. . .

... for a $C$-unit change in $x$

$$e^{C \cdot\widehat{\beta}_i - z^*_{1-\alpha/2} C \cdot SE(\widehat{\beta}_i)} \quad \text{to} \quad e^{C \cdot\widehat{\beta}_i + z^*_{1-\alpha/2} C \cdot SE(\widehat{\beta}_i)}$$


## fake news example

What impact does the *number of words in the title* have on the odds of being fake news?

```{r echo=FALSE}
tidy(news_mod, conf.int = TRUE) |> select(-statistic, -p.value)
```

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
Let's construct a 95% confidence interval for $\beta_1$: $\quad \widehat{\beta}_1 \pm z^*_{1-\alpha/2} SE(\widehat{\beta}_1)$
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
$z^*_{1-0.05/2} = z^*_{0.975} =$ 0.975 quantile from $N(0, 1)$ 
:::

::::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="35%"}
```{r}
qnorm(0.975)
```
:::
::::
:::::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}
$0.120 \pm 1.96 \cdot (0.0581) = (0.008,\ 0.237)$
:::


## fake news example

$0.120 \pm 1.96 \cdot (0.058) = (0.008,\ 0.237)$

<br>

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
Exponentiating the endpoints to get the CI for the odds ratio for a one-word increase in title length:

$$e^{0.008} = 1.008 \quad \text{to} \quad e^{0.237} = 1.267$$
:::
<br>

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
We are 95% confident that a one-word increase in title length is associated with an increase in the odds of being fake news by between 0.8% (a 1.008 factor increase) and  26.7% (a 1.267 factor increase), holding all other variables constant. 
:::


## fake news example

::: small
How do the odds of being fake news change for an increase of 10 words in the title length?

```{r echo=FALSE}
tidy(news_mod, conf.int = TRUE) |> select(-statistic, -p.value)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
:::{style="font-size:0.9em"}
95% CI: $\quad C \cdot \left[\widehat{\beta}_1 \pm z^*_{1-\alpha/2} SE(\widehat{\beta}_1)\right]$
:::
:::


::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
:::{style="font-size:0.9em"}
$\begin{split}
10 \left[0.120 \pm 1.96 \cdot (0.058) \right] &= (10\cdot(0.008),10\cdot(0.237))\\ &= (0.08, \ 2.37)\end{split}$
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3}
:::{style="font-size:0.9em"}
We are 95% confident that a 10-word increase in title length is associated with an increase in the odds of being fake news by between $e^{.08} = 1.08$ (an 8% increase) and a factor of $e^{2.37} = 10.69$ (a 1000% increase!), holding all other variables constant. 
:::
:::

# Pause for the most dramatic logistic regression story I've ever heard

# How can we tell if inference is correct?

## Recall

LINE conditions must be met for inference to be valid

- If Linearity fails, the line doesn't actually describe the relationship and everything breaks

- If INE fails, we can still interpret our coefficients (the geometry is still correct), but cannot trust inference
    - Confidence intervals too narrow
    - p-values too small

## What are the conditions for logistic regression model? 

1. **L**inear relationship between the log odds (logit) and the predictors

2. **I**ndependence: no pairs, clusters, etc.

3. **R**andomness: we have a random sample from the population or the data were collected from a randomized experiment

## Why not just plot $Y$ vs. $x$?

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
tibble(
  x = seq(0, 50, by = .5),
  log_odds = -0.9318 + 0.09772 * x,
  prob = exp(log_odds)/(1 + exp(log_odds))
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = prob)) + 
  geom_line(color = "#003300", linewidth = 1.5) + 
  geom_jitter(data = news, aes(x = title_caps_percent, y = type_num), height = .05, width = .1) +
  labs(x = "title_caps_percent", y = "Probability")
```

- Binary points pile up on two horizontal lines, so we can't "see" a trend
- We need to check whether the **log odds** is linear in $x$, not whether the probability is

## Empirical logits

If linearity holds, then $\text{logit}(\pi) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$, so the *observed* log odds for articles with similar $x$ should fall close to a line

::: incremental
1. Group the observations into bins of similar $x$ values (e.g., $g$ bins of about equal size)
2. In each bin, find the number of successes ($Y = 1$) and failures ($Y = 0$) and calculate the **empirical logit**
$$\log\left(\frac{\#\text{successes} + 0.5}{\#\text{failures} + 0.5}\right)$$
(the $0.5$ keeps us from taking the log of 0)
3. Plot the empirical logit against the mean $x$ in each bin
4. Look for a straight-line pattern
:::

```{r}
#| include: false
emp_logit_plot <- function(data, xvar, bins, xlab) {
  data |>
    mutate(bin = bins) |>
    group_by(bin) |>
    summarize(mean_x = mean({{ xvar }}),
              n = n(),
              successes = sum(type_num),
              emp_logit = log((successes + 0.5) / (n - successes + 0.5)),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    gf_point(emp_logit ~ mean_x, xlab = xlab, ylab = "Empirical logit") |>
    gf_lm(color = "#f15a31", linewidth = 1) 
}
```

## Empirical logit plot: `title_words`

- Using 13 bins (about 11-12 articles each)
- You will recreate this during the R activity today

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
emp_logit_plot(news, title_words, ntile(news$title_words, 13), "Mean title words in bin")
```

::: fragment
The points are noisy (each is based on only ~11 articles), but there is no clear curvature: a straight line is a reasonable summary
:::

## Empirical logit plot: `title_caps_percent`

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
emp_logit_plot(news, title_caps_percent, cut(news$title_caps_percent, c(-Inf, 0, 10, 15, 20, Inf)), "Mean % caps in bin")
```

- `r sum(news$title_caps_percent == 0)` of the 150 titles have **0%** capital letters, so equal-size bins won't work. We chose bins by hand: exactly 0, (0-10], (10-15], (15-20], and over 20
- Bins with only 6-12 articles are very noisy. Look at the overall trend, not individual points

## What to look for

::: medium
- **Roughly straight** trend &rarr; the linearity condition is reasonable
- **Curved** trend &rarr; try transforming $x$ (e.g., $\log x$) or adding a squared term
- Expect lots of scatter when bins are small; don't over-interpret one point
- These plots look at one predictor at a time (ignoring the others), so use Pearson residuals (next) to check linearity *after adjusting* for the other predictors
:::

## Categorical predictors

```{r}
news |>
  group_by(title_has_excl) |>
  summarize(n = n(), fake = sum(type_num), real = n - fake,
            `empirical logit` = log((fake + 0.5) / (real + 0.5))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

- With only two groups, two points always fall on a line, so there is no linearity condition to check for a binary predictor
- Empirical logits are still useful for *comparing* groups (e.g., color the points by `title_has_excl` to see whether we need an interaction)

## Pearson residuals

The raw difference between the observation (0 or 1) and the fitted probability is $y_i - \widehat \pi_i$

The **Pearson residual** standardizes that distance by the standard deviation of a 0/1 outcome with probability $\widehat \pi_i$:

$$r_{p_i} = \frac{y_i - \widehat \pi_i}{\sqrt{\widehat{\pi_i}(1-\widehat \pi_i)}}$$

::: small
Since $Y$ is 0 or 1, Pearson residuals for binary data are *not* approximately normal. We won't use a QQ plot, and we need a smoother to see any pattern
:::

## Pearson residuals in R 

- If the model is correct, then the expected (average) Pearson residual within each bin should be close to 0
- A smoother should be approximately horizontal line at 0

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 2.5
resid_panel(news_mod, plot = "resid", type = "pearson")
resid_panel(news_mod, plot = "resid", type = "pearson", smoother = TRUE)
```

## 

Smoothers can help draw attention to major flaws, but there will always be variation from the horizontal!

```{r}
#| cache: true
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-align: 'center'
#| message: false
library(nullabor) # lineup tools
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(051326)

N <- 1000
df <- tibble(
  x1 = rnorm(N),
  x2 = rnorm(N),
  prob_y = exp(-1 + x1 + x2 + 0.7 * x1^2) / 
    (1 + exp(-1 + x1 + x2 + 0.7 * x1^2)),
  y = rbinom(N, size = 1, prob = prob_y)
)

no_quad <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = df, family = "binomial")
no_quad_aug <- augment(no_quad, type.residuals = "pearson")

sim_ys <- simulate(no_quad, nsim = 19)
sim_aug <- map_dfr(
  sim_ys, 
  ~augment(glm(.x ~ x1 + x2, data = df, family = binomial))
)
sim_aug$.n <- rep(1:19, each = nrow(df))

no_quad_raw_lineup <- lineup(true = no_quad_aug, n = 19, samples = sim_aug) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(shape = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "darkorange") +
  facet_wrap(~.sample, ncol = 5) +
  labs(x = "Linear predictor", y = "Pearson residuals") +
  theme_bw()

no_quad_raw_lineup
```

::: footer
Only one of these datasets was simulated from the "wrong" distribution
:::

# Checking linearity is hard! 

## Independence

- We conduct inference assuming we have $n$ pieces of independent information from the $n$ data points 
- If the data points are dependent, we have *less* pieces of information than $n$ and our inference is overoptimistic
- Best to assess based on description of the data: 
    - Are they grouped in some way? 
    - Measurements over time?
    - Spatial component?
- The reason we make an index plot is to see if our data is ordered in some way

## Independence: index plot

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3
resid_panel(news_mod, plot = "index", type = "pearson")
```

## Randomness

> A dataset containing data behind the study "FakeNewsNet: A Data Repository with News Content, Social Context and Spatialtemporal Information for Studying Fake News on Social Media" https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.01286. The news articles in this dataset were posted to Facebook in September 2016, in the run-up to the U.S. presidential election.
